body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"Feedback on individual ordering to reduce routine preoperative testing: a controlled before-after study in six hospitals","authors":"Harrington-Oyelaran B, Mbeki-Lindholm S, Castro-Nakamura J","year":2020,"venue":"Ashcombe Journal of Health Services Improvement","doi":"10.5555/ajhsi.2020.0301","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Three hospitals gave surgeons and anaesthetists quarterly feedback on their own rates of routine preoperative testing in low-risk ambulatory surgery, compared with peers, and three similar hospitals did not. Over 18 months, electrocardiogram ordering fell from 48 to 29 percent in feedback hospitals and from 47 to 44 percent in comparison hospitals. Chest radiograph ordering fell in both groups. Same-day cancellations did not change. The effect was largest for clinicians whose baseline rates were highest. Hospitals were not allocated at random, and one feedback hospital also changed its pre-anaesthesia clinic during the study."},{"title":"Removing routine preoperative tests from electronic order sets: an interrupted time series","authors":"Solberg-Achebe K, Moreau-Kimani T","year":2022,"venue":"Kestrelmoor Clinical Informatics Letters","doi":"10.5555/kcil.2022.0115","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A regional health system removed chest radiographs and coagulation studies from the default preoperative order sets for low-risk ambulatory surgery, while leaving them available on request. Using 30 months of monthly data, we found an immediate fall in chest radiographs of 72 percent, sustained over 18 months after the change, and a 64 percent fall in coagulation studies. Tests ordered on request rose slightly. There was no change in same-day cancellations or in unplanned admissions within 30 days. The design cannot exclude other changes at the same time, but the size and timing of the fall make them an unlikely explanation."},{"title":"Multicomponent strategies to reduce low-value preoperative tests: a systematic review","authors":"Adeyemi-Pratt L, Holmberg-Ansah D, Tanaka-Oduya R, Fitzgerald-Silva M","year":2021,"venue":"Vellmar Evidence in Perioperative Care","doi":"10.5555/vepc.2021.0087","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched four databases for studies of strategies to reduce routine preoperative testing in low-risk surgery and included 26 studies, mostly before-after designs. Strategies that changed the ordering system, such as order set changes and electronic defaults, reduced testing more consistently than education or guidelines alone. Combinations of feedback and system changes produced the largest reductions. Only nine studies reported same-day cancellations and six reported perioperative complications, with no increase in either. Most studies were at high risk of bias, and effects beyond 12 months were rarely reported."},{"title":"Same-day cancellations after reducing routine preoperative testing in ambulatory surgery","authors":"Varga-Ellison P, Nkemelu-Strand A","year":2019,"venue":"Ashcombe Journal of Health Services Improvement","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"After a hospital stopped routine preoperative testing for healthy adults having ambulatory surgery, we compared same-day cancellations in the year before and the year after. Of 4,812 procedures before and 5,036 after, same-day cancellations were unchanged after routine tests were reduced (1.9 against 2.0 percent), and cancellations attributed to abnormal test results fell. Perioperative complications recorded in the surgical outcome register did not change. Surgeons initially expressed concern about cancellations, which fell away as the data were shared. The comparison is uncontrolled and covers one hospital."},{"title":"Nurse triage in the pre-anaesthesia clinic and preoperative test ordering: an observational study","authors":"Lindqvist-Obi S, Park-Hartmann K","year":2017,"venue":"Harthill Perioperative Nursing Reports","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared test ordering for low-risk ambulatory surgery patients assessed by nurse-led triage in the pre-anaesthesia clinic with patients assessed by junior doctors in the same clinic. Patients triaged by nurses using a structured protocol received at least one routine test in 22 percent of cases, against 57 percent of patients assessed by junior doctors. Nurses were more likely to follow the protocol and to document why a test was ordered. Allocation to nurse or doctor depended on clinic staffing on the day, and case mix differed slightly. The study did not report cancellations or complications."},{"title":"Why clinicians keep ordering low-value preoperative tests: an interview study with surgeons and anaesthetists","authors":"Rutherford-Mensah C, Esposito-Fairley L","year":2023,"venue":"Vellmar Evidence in Perioperative Care","doi":"10.5555/vepc.2023.0164","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We interviewed 28 surgeons and anaesthetists in four hospitals about routine preoperative testing. Clinicians knew the guidance but continued ordering because of habit, fear of blame if a problem was missed, and the belief that colleagues expected results to be available. Many said that tests were ordered by default before any clinician saw the patient. Several said that seeing their own ordering compared with peers had changed their practice more than education. Clinicians proposed removing tests from default order sets and agreeing locally who is responsible for deciding when a test is needed."},{"title":"Education alone and low-value preoperative test ordering: a comparison of hospitals","authors":"Brandt-Nwachukwu O, Sato-Mahlangu E","year":2016,"venue":"Harthill Perioperative Nursing Reports","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Four hospitals delivered an education programme on preoperative testing guidance to surgeons, anaesthetists and pre-anaesthesia clinic staff, and four comparable hospitals did not. Test ordering fell by about 10 percentage points in education hospitals in the first three months, but education alone produced no sustained reduction at twelve months, when ordering had returned to baseline. Comparison hospitals showed no change. Staff turnover meant that many clinicians at twelve months had not attended the education sessions. The authors conclude that education should be combined with changes to ordering systems."},{"title":"What patients expect from preoperative testing: a survey of adults awaiting ambulatory surgery","authors":"Kowalczyk-Adjei M, Delacroix-Hughes N","year":2024,"venue":"Kestrelmoor Clinical Informatics Letters","doi":"10.5555/kcil.2024.0022","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We surveyed 640 adults awaiting ambulatory surgery about their expectations of preoperative testing; 71 percent responded. Most respondents expected blood tests before surgery and believed that tests made surgery safer, but 64 percent said they would be comfortable without tests if their surgeon or anaesthetist explained why they were not needed. Older respondents and those with previous surgery were more likely to expect tests. Few respondents knew that tests could lead to further investigations and delays. Patient-facing explanations may support reductions in testing, but the survey did not test any intervention."}]}
